title: Citrus Nutrient Deficiency: Signs, Causes and the Fertilizer That Fixes It
metaTitle: Citrus Nutrient Deficiency: Signs and Fertilizer Fix
metaDescription: Citrus nutrient deficiency shows in the leaves. See the signs of nitrogen in citrus, dalandan or ponkan, how to be sure, and the fertilizer to apply.
excerpt: Citrus nutrient deficiency is one of the first things to check when the leaves of your citrus, dalandan or ponkan (citrus) turn yellow, purple or burnt at the edges. On Philippine farms the usual ones are nitrogen, potassium, zinc, magnesium, boron, manganese, iron, phosphorus and copper. This guide shows where each one starts, how to be sure, and the fertilizer that fixes it.

heroImage.alt: Orange leaf turned evenly pale yellow all over, from nitrogen shortage
heroImage.credit: Gómez Flores et al., CitrusUAT dataset, CC BY 4.0, via Zenodo

blocks.text: Start with one question: did the change begin on the old leaves or on the young ones? Nitrogen, potassium, magnesium and phosphorus move inside the plant, so a shortage shows on the old, lower leaves first. But zinc, boron, manganese, iron and copper stay where the plant first put them, so the young leaves and the growing tip show it first. After that, the color and the pattern narrow down which citrus nutrient deficiency you have, and a soil test confirms it. Each one below has its signs, its causes and its fix.
Citrus nutrient deficiency signs, old leaves and young leaves
Shows first on the old leaves

blocks.caption: Deficiencies that start on the old leaves of citrus, dalandan or ponkan
rows: old, lower leaves, the whole plant
Older leaves pale green to yellow and falling early, so the inside of the canopy goes bare.
old, lower leaves, leaf edges and tips
Old leaf edges yellow to bronze. Small fruit that split from the blossom end or show sunken creases in the peel.
Muriate of potash 0 0 60, Sulfate of potash 0 0 50
old, lower leaves, between the veins
Mature leaves next to the fruit yellow on both sides of the midrib, leaving a green V at the leaf base (bronzing).
old, lower leaves, fruit, grain or tubers
Rough fruit with a coarse, thick peel, a hollow core and sour juice. Old leaves dull with bronze freckles.

blocks.text: Shows first on the young leaves

blocks.caption: Deficiencies that start on the young leaves of citrus, dalandan or ponkan
rows: young leaves and the tip, between the veins
Young leaves mottled yellow between green veins, small, narrow and upright. Small, smooth, pale fruit.
fruit, grain or tubers, young leaves and the tip
Small, hard, lumpy fruit with gum pockets in the white peel. Many fruit drop. Shoot tips die and branch out.
young leaves and the tip, between the veins
Young and medium leaves light green between dark green vein bands. Leaves keep their size. Fruit pale and soft.
young leaves and the tip, between the veins
Newest leaves yellow to white with green veins. Tops of trees die back on wet or limey ground.
young leaves and the tip, fruit, grain or tubers
Brown gum stains on the fruit peel, fruit that split, and long, soft, S shaped shoots with big dark leaves.

blocks.text: Before you buy fertilizer for a citrus nutrient deficiency

So use the table to pick the likeliest citrus nutrient deficiency, then read its section below. Also keep in mind that dry soil, standing water, cold nights, a pest or a disease can look the same. That is why it pays to check the roots and the whole field first.
Nitrogen deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Orange leaf turned evenly pale yellow all over, from nitrogen shortage
blocks.caption: Photo: Gómez Flores et al., CitrusUAT dataset, CC BY 4.0, via Zenodo

blocks.text: Older leaves go pale green to yellow, with pale veins, and fall early. Yara notes a leaf can live only about 6 months instead of 1 to 3 years. So the inside of the canopy goes hollow. New leaves are small, thin and light green, and the whole tree looks evenly yellowish with no pattern. Trees bloom sparsely and set a light crop. The fruit peel is smooth and pale and the juice is lower in sugar and acid. You see it most at this stage: it shows most after flowering and before the rainy season. Trees often green up again in the rains if the crop is light. Heavy crops on unfed trees show it at any time.
Why nitrogen deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Low farm inputs, sandy soils low in organic matter, heavy rain or watering that leaches nitrogen, waterlogging, drought. Fresh straw or raw manure.
How to tell it apart

Late magnesium deficiency also yellows whole leaves. It shows during fruit growth and does not green again without magnesium. To be sure, leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from a flush on twigs without fruit, the way citrus is sampled, and a soil test. Even yellowing all over the tree, with no leaf pattern, points to nitrogen.
What to apply for nitrogen deficiency

Give a yearly dose of 200 grams of nitrogen, 100 grams of phosphate and 200 grams of potash per tree for citrus, split over the year. That much nitrogen is about 435 grams of Urea. For quick greening give a Urea spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every 15 days. Sprays of low biuret urea, calcium nitrate or potassium nitrate work fast. Weak or old trees do better with small, frequent doses.

Sold here with nitrogen: **Atlas Granular Urea** by Atlas Fertilizer Corporation (46 0 0), **YaraVera Viking Ship Granular Urea** by Yara Fertilizers Philippines, Inc. (46 0 0), **Planters Products Granular Urea** by Planters Products, Inc. (46 0 0) and **Harbest Granular Urea** by Harbest Agribusiness Corporation (46 0 0). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer), and the page on [nitrogen deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/nitrogen-deficiency) in every crop. In anee.io, Anee, the [smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician), reads a photo of the leaf and tells you which nutrient is short.
To keep it away, split nitrogen over the year and keep potash in step.
Potassium deficiency in citrus

The edges of older leaves turn pale yellow or bronze, and the yellow spreads over the leaf. On mandarins like ponkan, look for yellowing and bronzing with twisted, wrinkled leaves and spindly twigs. The top of the canopy thins. Fruit stay small with a smooth, thin peel, may split lengthwise from the blossom end, or show creasing, narrow sunken furrows in the peel. More fruit drop and the juice is weaker. You see it most at this stage: fruit growth, most of all in heavy crop years.
Why potassium deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Acid and sandy soils, heavy rain or watering, drought, soils rich in magnesium, limey soils. High nitrogen on heavy crops without enough potash.
How to tell it apart

Creasing can also come from low calcium or boron. Fruit that split around brown gum stains point to copper deficiency. To be sure, leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit, and a soil test for potash, magnesium and calcium. Count split and creased fruit per tree before and after feeding.
What to apply for potassium deficiency

Give 200 grams of potash (K2O) a year per bearing tree together with 200 grams of nitrogen and 100 grams of phosphate. 200 grams of potash is about 330 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60. Split it into two or three doses. For a quick fix give a Potassium nitrate spray at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) every two weeks.

Sold here with potassium: **Atlas Muriate of Potash** by Atlas Fertilizer Corporation (0 0 60), **Philphos Muriate of Potash** by Philippine Phosphate Fertilizer Corporation (0 0 60), **Harbest Granular Muriate of Potash** by Harbest Agribusiness Corporation (0 0 60) and **Swire Muriate of Potash** by Swire Agrotech Agricultural Products Inc. (0 0 60). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [potash fertilizer](/blog/potash-fertilizer), and the page on [potassium deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/potassium-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, keep potash in step with nitrogen every year, more so on heavy bearing trees.
Zinc deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Citrus leaves with yellow blotches between green veins, a zinc shortage pattern
blocks.caption: Photo: Scot Nelson (photo by Erika Magarifuji Location), CC0 1.0, via Flickr

blocks.text: Young leaves show yellow patches between the veins with an uneven green band along the midrib and main veins (mottle leaf). In severe cases leaves are pointed, narrow, upright and very small (little leaf), twigs thin out and die back. The outer canopy looks dead while the centre stays dense. Fruit on weak twigs are small with a smooth, pale, thin skin and little juice. While water sprouts on the main limbs carry normal leaves and big, coarse fruit. Flowering and fruit set drop. You see it most at this stage: new flushes. Worse on trees with a heavy crop and weak roots.
Why zinc deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
High pH and limed soils, soils high in phosphorus or given heavy phosphate, organic soils, heavy poultry manure, and too much nitrogen. Magnesium or copper shortage can also cut zinc uptake.
How to tell it apart

Citrus greening (huanglongbing, HLB) also gives a yellow mottle between the veins. HLB and tristeza are the main causes of low citrus production in the country. To be sure, do the pen test, then spray zinc on a few branches and watch the next flush. If blotches stay uneven or the tree keeps declining, send leaves for an HLB laboratory test.
What to apply for zinc deficiency

Spray zinc on each new flush when leaves are two thirds to almost fully expanded. Give Zinc sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) mixed with 1 percent lime (10 grams per liter) every two weeks. Zinc on the soil rarely pays on acid soils and does not work on limey soils.

Sold here with zinc: **Harvester Zinc Sulphate Heptahydrate** by Universal Harvester, Inc. (22 percent zinc), **Great Planters Zinc Sulphate Heptahydrate** by Agway Chemicals Corp. (21 percent zinc), **Zinc Sulphate Monohydrate** by Petbowe Trading Corporation (33 percent zinc) and **YaraVita ZINTRAC 700** by Yara Fertilizers Philippines, Inc. (40 percent zinc). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [fertilizer with zinc](/blog/micronutrients-for-rice), and the page on [zinc deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/zinc-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, keep the pH below 6.5, avoid heavy phosphate and poultry manure, and include zinc in the regular spray program.
Magnesium deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Citrus branch with yellow older leaves, green at the base, from magnesium shortage
blocks.caption: Photo: Florida Division of Plant Industry, Florida Department of Agriculture, CC BY 3.0 US, via ipmimages.org

blocks.text: Leaves look normal on the new flush, then mature leaves close to the growing fruit show yellow blotches near the base on each side of the midrib. The blotches join until only the tip and a V shaped area at the base, pointing up the midrib, stay green. In acute cases the whole leaf turns yellow or bronze and drops. Heavily fruited limbs can lose nearly all their leaves while lightly loaded limbs stay green. Fruit are lower in sugar, acid and vitamin C, and seedy kinds swing into alternate bearing. You see it most at this stage: fruit growth and maturing, on heavily bearing limbs.
Why magnesium deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Sandy and acid soils, soils rich in potash or given heavy potash, and cold, wet periods. On limey soils high calcium holds magnesium back.
How to tell it apart

Nitrogen deficiency yellows the whole tree evenly and often greens again in the rains. Magnesium yellowing does not, without magnesium. To be sure, leaf test of 4 to 6 month old leaves from twigs without fruit, and a soil test for magnesium, potash and calcium. Signs worst on the heaviest fruiting limbs point to magnesium.
What to apply for magnesium deficiency

On acid to neutral soils, Dolomite corrects mild cases. Where the soil test shows low magnesium, give magnesium at a rate equal to 20 percent of the nitrogen rate, from Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) or Kieserite. On limey soils use magnesium sprays on the leaves.

Sold here with magnesium: **Dolomite** by A6 Agrisource Limited Corporation (24 percent calcium and 11 percent magnesium), **YaraTera KRISTA MgS** by Yara Fertilizers Philippines, Inc. (16 percent MgO and 13 percent sulfur), **Magnepro** by Ramgo International Corporation (16 percent MgO and 12.8 percent sulfur) and **Lucky Planters Magnesium Sulphate Heptahydrate (Epsom Salt)** by Mindanao Agriplus Corporation (16.27 percent MgO and 13 percent sulfur). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [complete fertilizer](/blog/complete-fertilizer-14-14-14), and the page on [magnesium deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/magnesium-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, lime with dolomite, keep potash and magnesium in balance, and avoid very heavy crops on weak trees.
Boron deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Ponkan fruits that stayed small, hard and lumpy with greenish patches from boron shortage
blocks.caption: Photo: Yang et al., Plants (MDPI) 2021, CC BY 4.0, via the publisher

blocks.text: Fruit show it most: small, hard and misshapen with a lumpy surface, with gum pockets and dark spots in the white inner peel (albedo) near the rind and sometimes in the core, and gum on the skin. Many fruit drop, peel can crease, and fruit rot more after harvest. The growing tip dies and the shoot sends out many side shoots. Young leaves wilt early, show water soaked spots, curl, and the veins split and turn corky. You see it most at this stage: flowering to fruit growth, often after a long dry spell.
Why boron deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Sandy and alkaline soils low in organic matter, high nitrogen or calcium, cold wet weather and drought. Programs that use only high analysis fertilizers without micronutrients.
How to tell it apart

Citrus greening also gives corky veins and small, lopsided fruit that color unevenly. Check leaves with the pen test. To be sure, leaf test and soil test for boron. Cut open a few fruit to look for gum and dark spots in the albedo.
What to apply for boron deficiency
Give a Borax spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter). Use boron each year where needed, on the soil or as a spray but never both, since citrus is easily burned by excess boron.

Sold here with boron: **Solubor** by Caldic Philippines Inc. (21 percent boron), **Etifert 11 (Borax Decahydrate)** by Zetryl.Chem Phils., Inc. (11 percent boron), **YaraVita BORTRAC 150** by Yara Fertilizers Philippines, Inc. (11.1 percent boron) and **Grow More Liquid Chelate Boron** by Sagrex Corporation (10 percent boron). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer), and the page on [boron deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/boron-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, use fertilizers that carry micronutrients, keep organic matter up, and water in long dry spells.
Manganese deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Orange leaf with pale yellow patches between broad green vein bands, from manganese shortage
blocks.caption: Photo: Gómez Flores et al., CitrusUAT dataset, CC BY 4.0, via Zenodo

blocks.text: Young leaves show a fine net of green veins on a lighter green background. By full size there are dark green bands along the midrib and main veins with light green to yellow areas between. In bad cases white or grey spots form between the veins and leaves drop early, but leaf size and shape stay normal. The crop is smaller, and fruit are smaller, softer and paler in color. With zinc shortage it forms marl chlorosis: dark veins with dull white and green between. You see it most at this stage: young and newly matured flushes. Mild signs can fade as leaves harden.
Why manganese deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Acid soils, where manganese leaches, and limey or overlimed soils, where it is locked up. Sandy and organic soils and cold, wet periods add to it.
How to tell it apart

Zinc deficiency makes leaves small, narrow and pointed. Iron deficiency is paler, with a finer net, on the newest leaves. To be sure, watch the leaves over a few weeks, since mild signs can pass. Then do a leaf test and a soil test for pH and manganese.
What to apply for manganese deficiency

Give a Manganese sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Spray when the new flush is two thirds to fully expanded. A little low biuret urea in the tank helps uptake. On acid soils manganese sulfate can also go on the soil, but not on limey soils.

Sold here with manganese: **Manganese Sulfate** by Zetryl.Chem Phils., Inc. (31 percent manganese), **Tierramino Mn** by Unilox Far East Resources Inc. (12 percent manganese and 7 percent N), **Multimate** by Agway Chemicals Corp. (1.8 percent Mn, 2.8 percent Zn, 4 percent N, 4.5 percent S (w/v)) and **Biozome** by Manchem Industries, Inc. (12 percent S, 12 percent Zn, 3 percent Mn, 1 percent Mg, 1 percent Fe, 1 percent Cu, 0.5 percent B, 0.05 percent Mo). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer), and the page on [manganese deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/manganese-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, avoid overliming and include manganese with zinc in the regular sprays.
Iron deficiency in citrus

blocks.alt: Citrus leaves: yellow leaves with green veins from iron shortage, compared with healthy dark green leaves
blocks.caption: Photo: Florida Division of Plant Industry, Florida Department of Agriculture, CC BY 3.0 US, via ipmimages.org

blocks.text: It starts on the youngest leaves: yellow green, then pale yellow between veins that stay green, sometimes like a fine net. In acute cases leaves are small, very thin and fragile and shed early. The tree dies back hard at the top and outer edge, sometimes with a dead top over normal lower limbs. It may hit only one branch or a few trees. Fruit are small, hard, coarse and light colored, with weaker juice. You see it most at this stage: new flushes, mainly on wet or limey ground.
Why iron deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
High pH and limey soils (lime induced chlorosis), over watering, prolonged wet soil, poor drainage, cool soil, excess salts, high phosphorus. Copper built up in old orchard soils.
How to tell it apart

Manganese and zinc shortage often come with it. Flood damage to roots and copper toxicity both show first as iron chlorosis. To be sure, soil test for pH, and for copper on old orchard land. Check drainage and look at the roots.
What to apply for iron deficiency

Improve drainage and watering first. Trees helped or cured by that alone. On high pH soils apply an iron chelate (Fe EDDHA) to the soil. Iron sprays on citrus green the leaves only in specks and can burn leaves and fruit, so if you try one, keep it to a Ferrous sulfate spray at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter), twice, two weeks apart.

Sold here with iron: **Ferrous Sulphate Heptahydrate** by Cleveland Industries Inc. (20 percent iron), **Ferrous Sulfate Monohydrate** by Zetryl.Chem Phils., Inc. (30 percent iron), **Grow More Liquid Chelate Iron with Sulfur** by Sagrex Corporation (5 percent iron and 3 percent sulfur) and **Biozome** by Manchem Industries, Inc. (12 percent S, 12 percent Zn, 3 percent Mn, 1 percent Mg, 1 percent Fe, 1 percent Cu, 0.5 percent B, 0.05 percent Mo). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer), and the page on [iron deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/iron-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, plant on well drained ground, avoid overliming, and keep pH near neutral.
Phosphorus deficiency in citrus

Leaf signs are weak. Older leaves lose their deep green, partly yellow. May show a dull purplish or bronze cast or small bronze freckles along the main veins. Leaves and fruit drop early and flowering is poor. The clearest sign is the fruit: rough, with a coarse, thick peel, a hollow core and high acid, ripening late. You see it most at this stage: young trees and new plantings on land never fertilized. Rare where trees have been fed phosphorus for years.
Why phosphorus deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
Strongly acid soils where iron and aluminium lock phosphorus up, limey soils where calcium does, low organic matter, cold wet soil and weak roots.
How to tell it apart

Potassium deficiency gives the opposite fruit: small, with a smooth, thin peel. Nitrogen deficiency gives evenly pale leaves without bronze freckles. To be sure, soil test for available phosphorus and pH, and a leaf test.
What to apply for phosphorus deficiency

Apply a phosphorus fertilizer, following the soil test. The usual yearly citrus dose includes 100 grams of phosphate per tree. Superphosphate suits soils of any pH and adds sulfur. Warns against DAP (18 46 0) on alkaline soils. Lime very acid soils so phosphorus stays available.

Sold here with phosphorus: **Triple Super Phosphate** by Newman Chemicals Corporation (0 46 0), **Sagrex Duofos Granular Guano Phosphate** by Sagrex Corporation (0 22 0 (guano phosphate)), **Philphos 18 46 0** by Philippine Phosphate Fertilizer Corporation (18 46 0 (diammonium phosphate)) and **Atlas Di Ammonium Phosphate** by Atlas Fertilizer Corporation (18 46 0). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [16 20 0 fertilizer](/blog/16-20-0-fertilizer), and the page on [phosphorus deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/phosphorus-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, put phosphorus in the planting hole and in the first years on new land, and add compost.
Copper deficiency in citrus

On oranges the fruit often show it first: brown stained areas of hard gum on the peel that darken to almost black by half size, fruit splitting across or around the stains, and heavy fruit drop. Leaves come out unusually large and dark green with the midrib bowed up, on long, soft, angular, drooping S shaped shoots. Clear gum blisters form at the nodes, reddish brown gum breaks out on twigs. Twigs die back and sprout bunches of weak buds. You see it most at this stage: young trees and new plantings, and trees pushed with heavy nitrogen.
Why copper deficiency happens in citrus, dalandan or ponkan
New plantings on sandy or organic soils never farmed, limey soils, and heavy nitrogen (it is also called ammoniation). It is rare where copper fungicides are used.
How to tell it apart

Normal splitting starts only at the blossom end. Copper splits also run across the fruit and around gum stains. To be sure, check the spray record. Copper deficiency is unlikely where copper fungicides are sprayed.
What to apply for copper deficiency

Near immediate recovery and normal fruit set from a copper spray at flowering. Give Copper sulfate at 0.5 percent (5 grams per liter) every two weeks. Try a few branches first, since plain copper sulfate can burn soft leaves. Cut back excess nitrogen. Below pH 5.5 built up soil copper can kill roots, so do not overdo it.

Sold here with copper: **Omex Zynergy** by Jardine Distribution, Inc. (3.75 percent zinc and 2.11 percent copper), **Grower's Choice Copper Sulphate Pentahydrate** by Zetryl.Chem Phils., Inc. (25 percent copper and 12 percent sulfur), **Agsmart Copper Sulphate** by AgSmart Corporation (25 percent copper and 12 percent sulfur) and **Liquid Chelate Copper w/ Sulfur** by Sagrex Corporation (5 percent copper and 2 percent sulfur). Check the FPA registration on the bag and follow the label rate. For the how and when, see our guide to [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer), and the page on [copper deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/copper-deficiency) in every crop.
To keep it away, on new sandy land add copper to the fertilizer at 2.5 percent of the nitrogen rate.

blocks.title: Let a soil test decide the rate
blocks.text: A soil test is the surest check for any citrus nutrient deficiency. Before you buy, ask your Municipal Agriculture Office where to send a soil sample. The DA regional soil laboratories test soil, and the result says how much of each fertilizer your citrus, dalandan or ponkan needs. That saves money, because extra fertilizer is money lost.

blocks.text: Citrus nutrient deficiency questions

items.q: Why are my citrus, dalandan or ponkan leaves turning yellow?
items.a: The most common cause is nitrogen deficiency: older leaves pale green to yellow and falling early, so the inside of the canopy goes bare. If the young leaves turn yellow first instead, look at zinc deficiency.

items.q: What fertilizer fixes nitrogen deficiency in citrus?
items.a: Give a yearly dose of 200 grams of nitrogen, 100 grams of phosphate and 200 grams of potash per tree for citrus, split over the year. That much nitrogen is about 435 grams of Urea.

items.q: What fertilizer fixes potassium deficiency in citrus?
items.a: Give 200 grams of potash (K2O) a year per bearing tree together with 200 grams of nitrogen and 100 grams of phosphate. 200 grams of potash is about 330 grams of Muriate of potash 0 0 60.

items.q: What fertilizer fixes zinc deficiency in citrus?
items.a: Spray zinc on each new flush when leaves are two thirds to almost fully expanded. Give Zinc sulfate at 2 percent (20 grams per liter) mixed with 1 percent lime (10 grams per liter) every two weeks.

items.q: How do I know which nutrient my citrus, dalandan or ponkan lacks?
items.a: First look at where the change began, on the old leaves or the young ones, then at the color and the pattern. Next, confirm the citrus nutrient deficiency with a soil test or a leaf test before you buy fertilizer.
